analytic.title: Time Constrained Message Transmission in a LAN Environment

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: We study the problem of transmitting time constrained synchronous messages in local a n a networks. A bandwidth allocation scheme for synchronous messages is developed and the suficient condition for schedulability is derived. Implementation of the allocation scheme is proposed on slotted ring and DQDB networks.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: In a hard real-time system, a failure to observe the timing constraints can result in intolerable system degradation and, in some cases, catastrophic consequences. The inherent characteristics of many such s'ystems require that multiple, autonomous computers, connected through a local area network (LAN), cooperate in a distributed fashion. In such an environment, the end-toend deadlines on computations executing on multiple computers require time-constrained message transmission. These messages, known as synchronous messages, are periodically generated and are subject to real-time constraints.

In recent years significant advances have been made in the area of real-time communication scheduling [2, 1, 4, 10, 12, 13, 15, 141. In many cases, the approach taken is to emulate centralized scheduling and exploit well known results from uniprocessor scheduling. However, the scheduling of hard real-time messages in a lo-.cal area network is inherently different due to its distributed nature. As a result, significant overheads may result in attempting to maintain accurate global information. To make the solutions scalable to large systems with high speed transmission media, it is critical that the real-time communication schemes operate with minimal global state information.

The protocols developed in recent years may be classified into three classes [6] In this paper, we consider the problem of guaranteeing timing constraints for synchronous tr&c on slotted ring and DQDB networks, both of which use slots as unit of transmission. We propose a bandwidth allocation scheme for real-time communication. The scheme divides the time frame into allocation cycles, and attempts to satisfy the average requirements of each stream in every allocation cycle. The challenge of the problem lies in the fact that the bandwidth must be allocated in integral units (slots), while the average bandwidth requirement may be non-integral. The naive a p proach of satisfying the average requirement in every cycle (i.e., by allocating the ceiling of the bandwidth required) may result in significant over-allocation. To counter this, we use an approach similar to [5] in the context of pre-run-time scheduling of hard real-time tasks in a multi-processor environment. We derive a simple schedulability condition for the allocation scheme and propose implementation of the scheme on the aforementioned networks with minimal additional overhead.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. The systems and the traffic model is described in section 2. The bandwidth allocation scheme and its properties are discussed in section 3. We propose slot access mechanisms to implement the bandwidth allocation scheme in section 4 and the provide some concluding remarks in section 5.

div.head: System and Traffic Model
div.p: We consider a system of multiple computers connected via a LAN. For our discussion, the LAN is assumed to be a slotted ring [3] or a DQDB [7]. We assume that there are N streams of synchronous messages, SI, Sz, . . . , S N .

Each stream is periodic. The period of a stream Si is Pi. A message arrives at the beginning of its period and must be transmitted by the end of the period. Messages are packetiseda packet fits into the payload of a slot. The maximum length of a message from stream Si is Ci , denoting the number of slots required to transmit the memage. Note that Ci is an integer. All streams are assumed to be in-phase, i.e., their first message arrives at time 0.

We say that a given set of synchronous message streams is schcdulablc if there exists a mechanism which guarantees the transmission of all synchronous meseages within their deadlines. We aasume that there is a virtual station for each message stream. In the rest of the discussion we will use terms stream and station interchangeably.

div.head: Synchronous Bandwidth Allocation Scheme
div.p: In this section, we present a bandwidth allocation scheme and discuss some of its properties. For details the reader is referred to [8,11]. The scheme is presented without regard to its implementation.

In our scheme the timeline is divided into fixed length intervals. Each such interval denotes an allocation cycle. Let L denote the length of the allocation cycle. Scaling the slot transmission time to one time unit, L also denotes the number of slots available for data transmission in an allocation cycle. To simplify the discussion, we assume that L exactly divides Pi. The allocation of bandwidth to different streams, within each allocation cycle, must be done in a manner that guarantees the transmission of each message before its deadline. The scheme does not make any assumption about when a slot is allocated to a message. Hence, if a message is allocated a slot in allocation cycle k, then it must have arrived before the beginning of the cycle and must have a deadline after the end of the cycle.

To ensure that the message is transmitted within its deadline, we must ensure that Ci slots are allocated to the message within Pi/L allocation cycles. Thus, the average (per-cycle) requirement of a message stream Si is given by & = LCi/Pi = LUi, where Vi = Ci/Pi.
In general, the requirement may be non-integral. Let U = xEi Vi.

Let & = Ii + Fi where, Ii = L&J and Fi = {a}. Ii and Fi are the integral and fractional part of the band-width requirement, respectively1. The integral part of the bandwidth requirement can be satisfied by allocating l i slots to the meagage Si. However, a fraction of a slot cannot be allocated to the message. The simplest way to get around thia problem is to allocate slots to message Si in every cycle. Thia scheme may allocate significantly more slots than required, and may severely deteriorate message schedulability (i.e. , schedule less streams than that can be accommodated). The propcsed allocation scheme avoids this over-allocation by carefully adjusting the slot allocations in each cycle.

The idea behind the allocation algorithm is as follows. Out of the L slots in an allocation cycle, the i n t e gral slot requirements of all messages are satisfied first. Of the remaining slots, some messages with fractional requirements are allocated one slot each, while fractional requirements of others are left unsatisfied. Slot requirements for the next cycle are suitably adjusted to compensate for this unfair allocation.

Thus, a necessary condition for schedulability is that the aggregated integral requirements never exceed the number of slots. The following theorem states the schedulability condition.

div.head: Implement at ion
div.p: In the previous section, we have developed an allocation scheme which guarantees the timely transmission of synchronous messages, so long as the utilization bounds are satisfied. However, the scheme, as described, requires a centralized implementation. In this section, we briefly describe how the bandwidth allocation scheme can be implemented in a distributed manner on slotted ring and DQDB networks. The details may be obtained from [8, 111.

div.head: DQDB Network
div.p: In this section we describe the implementation of the allocation scheme on a DQDB network. We present two schemesone using Pre-Arbitrated slots and the other one using Queued Arbitrated slots.

div.head: Pre-Arbitrated Slot Allocation
div.p: The connection-oriented pre-arbitrated service of DQDB is achieved by scheduling of slots through a central scheduler. The use of a centralized scheduler makes the implementation of the bandwidth allocation scheme relatively straightforward.

In order to set up, tear down and maintain a connection, the signaling termination, the bandwidth manager, the VCI server and the slot scheduler need to communicate among themselves. We assume, for simplicity, that these entities are co-located at the head of the bus and refer to them collectively as the connection manager (CM). The CM treats each message stream as a connection between the source and destination and assigns a VCI to it. The CM maintains all required information regarding the live connections (connection id, source and destination pairs, initial and kth cycle requirements, & and $, respectively) in an Allocation Table . At the beginning of each cycle, the CM executes the allocation algorithm and determines the number of slots to be allocated for each connection (i.e. VCI). It generates the PA slots accordingly by stamping them with appropriate VCIs.

In order to setup a new connection with another station, the source sends a call setup request to the CM specifying the stream parameters. Let the new stream be S = (C,P). Upon receiving the request the CM determines the average bandwidth requirement of the stream per allocation cycle as shown in section 3. If R + & 5 L , where L is the number of slots available in a cycle, then the connection is accepted and a new VCI is assigned. The VCI is communicated to the source and the destination of the connection and a new connection is set up. If the schedulability test fails the request for connection is denied.

A connection can be cleared either by the source or by the destination. The request to clear a connection is sent to the CM which responds by deleting the corresponding entry from the Allocation Table and notifying the hosts to delete the VCI from their tables.

div.head: Queued Arbitrated Slot Allocation
div.p: In this section we discuss an implementation of the bandwidth allocation scheme using the QA slots. Since the operation of the two buses is identical, we will concentrate on the operation of the F-Bus for transmitting messages. Requests for message transmission on the F-Bus are made on the R-Bus. To simplify the discussion, we consider an abstraction of the DQDB architecture. In this abstraction, the slots are generated by the slot generator on the R-Bus, at regular intervals. When the slots reach the end of the bus, they appear on the F-Bus (perhaps, after some delay). Since the slots on the F-Bus are generated at the same rate as the R-Bus, such an abstraction is easy to d i e v e . In our abstraction, we will also consider the slots to be numbered for ease of exposition.

We consider an allocation cycle of length L', of which at least L slots are marked QA. Consider the allocation of slots in a particular allocation cycle. Let the slots be numbered 1,2,. . . , L , . . . , L', of which slots 1,. . . , L are available for use during the current allocation cycle for transmission of real-time messages using this scheme. The remaining slots may be used either as pre-arbitrated slots, or for other (e.g., non real-time) messages.

Due to propagation delays, the slots arrive at different nodes at different timeshence, there is a phase lag between the allocation cycles at different nodes. At each node, we consider the allocation cycle to be com- Let a stream Si = (Ci, Pi), be associated with each node i. As before, let the requirement of stream S j in the cycle being considered be ri slots, such that rj = nj + fj, where hj and fi are the integral and fractional requirements, respectively. We show how the algorithm allocate can be implemented in a distributed manner using the QA slots. To be able to implement the algorithm in a distributed manner, each node must be capable of deciding (i) when to use a slot for transmission, and (ii) whether it can use an extra slot for its fractional requirement. Each node independently determines its requirements at the beginning of each allocation cycle. The requirements are indicated to nodes downstream on the R-Bus, using the Request bits in the slots.

The scheme requires two priority levels to distinguish between requests for integral requirements and fractional requirements. We will refer to the two levels as H (high) and L (low). Each node maintains a queue for transmission, one for each priority level. The allocation algorithm for an allocation cycle is described below:

(a) Integral requirements are requested at priority level H. Fractional requirements are requested at priority level L. The requirements for the current cycle are calculated at the beginning of the cycle.

(b) At the beginning of each cycle, any pending request at the priority level L is discarded. Recall that in the allocation algorithm not all streams may satisfy the fractional requirements. The requests remaining at priority level L are the requests that could not be sat-S e d in the current cycle. Since, the requests in the subsequent cycle are adjusted accordingly, the queue at priority level L must be cleared. We note that for BUG (i) If the slot is already used, then the node lets the slot go by and makes no changes in its queues.
(ii) If the slot is free and there is a pending request at H-Level then the station removes the request from the queue, and lets the slot go free.
(iii) If the slot is free, the queue at level H is empty and it has not completed its integral requirements, then the node uses the slot and decrements its integral requirements by 1.
(iv) If the slot is free, the queue at level H is empty, and there is a pending request at level L, then the node lets the slot go and removes one request from the queue.
(v) If the slot is free, the queues at level H and L are empty, and the node has completed its integral requirements, it uses the slot for transmission if fi > 0.
If fi = 0, or the node has already used a slot for fractional requirement, then the slot may be used for a non real-time message.

As a result of the protocol, the integral requirements of each etream are satisfied first, from SN to SI. When the integral requirements are satisfied, the fractional r e quirements are satisfied starting from SN until either (i) all streams satisfy their fractional requirements, or (ii) all available slots in the current cycle are used up. To ensure that the protocol operates successfully, the requests for a cycle must be computed before the new cycle starts. Specifically, at the beginning of the request phase, the requirements must be known. Since, the requirements may not be known until the transmission phase of the previous cycle is overan added restriction is that the request phase in a cycle must not start until the transmission phase of the previous cycle is finished at all nodes. Depending on the propagation delays, this may restrict the number of slots that may be made available in each allocation cycle for real-time

div.head: 5-Concluding Remarks
div.p: We presented a bandwidth allocation echeme for time critical periodic measages. The allocation scheme guar- antees timely delivery of messages. A schedulability test for the proposed allocation scheme was derived. We p r e posed the implementation of the scheme on slotted ring network with minimal additional overhead and loss of schedulable utilization. We also presented two implementations of the allocation scheme on a DQDB network. The first implementation uses prearbitrated ac-ce88 to the transmission medium and provides a simple mechanism to guarantee timely transmission of periodic messages. It requires no modification to the current standard. The other implementation uses queued arbitrated slots. It prevents capacity wastage when the streams use less than the reserved bandwidth. However, the implementation using QA slots is more complex, and requires minor changes in the standard.
